relations.note: As Ehecatl, Quetzalcoatl clears the roads before Tlaloc produces rain.
After Quetzalcoatl retrieves maize, the Tlaloque help release the mountain's remaining food stores.
As a great serpent, Quetzalcoatl seizes and tears Tlaltecuhtli apart with Tezcatlipoca.
Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca tear the earth being apart to form earth and heaven.
Quetzalcoatl and several gods look east before Nanahuatzin rises as the Sun.
They pursue the hidden pair and devour Mayahuel's branch while Quetzalcoatl survives.
Xipe and Ehēcatl correctly identify the east as the sunrise direction.

relations.myth: Regeneration of maize and the Fifth Sun
relations.note: Modern scholarship links them symbolically; no continuous early narrative joins them.
A later colored-Tezcatlipoca systematization makes Xipe and Quetzalcoatl brothers.
relations.source: Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: A disputed interpretation identifies Quetzalcoatl emerging from one rim serpent beside Xiuhtecuhtli.
Quetzalcoatl appears opposite the Xochipilli-Cinteotl side; the scene’s meaning remains disputed.
Xolotl accompanies or doubles Quetzalcoatl in variants of the underworld journey.
Xolotl is Quetzalcoatl’s canine manifestation, nahualli, alter ego, or divine counterpart.
Xolotl repeatedly hides from Ehēcatl's divine sacrifice but is eventually caught.

relations.myth: Retrieval of ancestral bones from Mictlan
relations.note: Modern syntheses make Xolotl Quetzalcoatl’s companion, but the core Nahuatl passage is ambiguous.
relations.source: Leyenda de los Soles and later retellings

relations.note: Some traditions treat Xolotl and Quetzalcoatl as twins or nahual-counterparts.
Later scholars identify Yacatecuhtli as a merchant aspect of Quetzalcoatl.
Nācxitl, a title of Quetzalcoatl, is listed with Yacatecuhtli among merchant gods.
Later systematization pairs Tonatiuh as the present sun with Tecciztecatl as moon.
Xolotl evades divine death through transformations after Tecciztecatl has become the moon.
Tecuciztecatl becomes the moon before Xolotl resists the collective divine sacrifice.
Tepeyollotl is interpreted as Tezcatlipoca’s jaguar form or nāhualli.
Manuscript attributes closely join this jaguar night and cave power with Tezcatlipoca.
Tlaloc and Tepeyollotl occupy the northern quarter together.
Tlaloc and Tepeyollotl are co-members of the rotating night-patron sequence.
Tlazolteotl appears as a secondary or paired patron with Tepeyollotl.
Tlazolteotl and Tepeyollotl are co-members of the rotating night-patron sequence.
Colonial commentary links her feast days to Tepeyollotl’s trecena without clarifying their relationship.
A masked Venus manifestation spears a figure commonly identified as Tezcatlipoca.
Colonial traditions present an unstable rivalry between Tezcatlipoca and Tlaloc over Xochiquetzal.
Tezcatlipoca’s ordering of the earth is connected with Tlaloc’s emergence.
Systematized versions associate Tezcatlipoca with installing Tlaloc as the third sun.
Creator gods install Tlaloc as ruler of a later sun; Tezcatlipoca's role varies.
relations.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: Tezcatlipoca takes Xochiquetzal after she is associated as Tlaloc’s wife.
Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl attack and tear apart the many-mouthed earth being.
Tezcatlipoca helps restrain and dismember Tlaltecuhtli, forming earth and heaven from the body.
Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl transform her divided body into the ordered earth.
Tlazolteotl and Tezcatlipoca jointly occupy the trecena's principal almanac panel.
Titlacahuan joins the divine gathering following the solar confrontation.
Some colonial classifications place him among beings translated as tzitzimime, without a narrative encounter.
Some cosmologies and reconstructions associate him with the disputed Red Tezcatlipoca.
A later colored-Tezcatlipoca systematization makes Xipe and Tezcatlipoca brothers.
relations.source: Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: Some codical images place Xiuhcoatl-like insignia on Tezcatlipoca's back without explanatory narrative.
Unstable later traditions describe a sexual or marital appropriation of Xochiquetzal.
A woman embodying Xochiquetzal ceremonially accompanies Tezcatlipoca's impersonator as a wife.
A woman embodying Xochiquetzal becomes one ceremonial wife of his impersonator.
She transgresses sexually with Tezcatlipoca, possibly interpreted as Piltzintecuhtli.
Later chronicles say Tezcatlipoca took Xochiquetzal from Tlaloc.
Tezcatlipoca steals her from Tlaloc and carries her above the nine heavens.
They appear within the same pictorial sequence, though no discrete encounter is certain.
Modern scholarship sometimes identifies Yacatecuhtli with Tezcatlipoca through shared traits and insignia.
Durán lists Titlacahuan among the arriving companion lords called Yacateuctin.
He shoots at the motionless new Sun, misses, and is struck back.

relations.myth: Morning Star attacks the enthroned Sun
relations.note: The Morning Star shoots first and misses; Tonatiuh's answering dart strikes him.
Tonatiuh strikes his face, causing his transformation into Itztlacoliuhqui.
Tonatiuh's answering attack transforms or disables the wounded Morning Star.
Modern scholarship proposes convergence between Xiuhcoatl's fire-serpent form and Morning Star light-serpent imagery.
Later astronomical reconstructions contrast evening-star Xolotl with the dawn or Morning-Star deity.

relations.myth: Creation of the small rain ministers
relations.note: Tlaloc creates the smaller rain ministers who carry and pour his jars.
relations.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: Directional rain figures surround and pluralize the central rain power identified with Tlaloc.
The Tlaloque are Tlaloc’s subordinate rain beings, assistants, or distributed manifestations.
The Tlaloque obey Tlaloc and distribute the different waters stored in his dwelling.
relations.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: They strike or break water vessels, producing thunder, lightning, and varied rains.
Colonial authors sometimes apply Earth Lord terminology to Tlaloc, reflecting overlapping terrestrial, mountain, and water domains.
Rain- and storm-bearing aerial Tzitzimime overlap his functions, without a documented meeting.
Tláloc's rain rites surrounded Xipe's festival, whose hymn invokes water and rain.
The Ríos tradition associates Xochiquetzal as Tlaloc’s wife.
Xochiquetzal is Tlaloc's wife before Tezcatlipoca abducts her.
The hymn associates Yacatecuhtli with Tlalocan, sustenance, and its jade chest.
This descriptive sacred-earth name is sometimes equivalent to Tlaltecuhtli, depending on the passage.
Some scholars identify the central face as Tlaltecuhtli or a combined earth-sun being rather than Tonatiuh alone.
Modern iconographic analysis proposes a Tonatiuh-Tlaltecuhtli fusion in the Sun Stone.

relations.myth: Swallowing and birth of the sun
relations.note: Tlaltecuhtli swallows the setting sun, participates in its nocturnal transformation, and births it at dawn.
Shared posture, claws, devouring mouth, and generative force support contested iconographic convergence.
Yacatecuhtli's merchant worshippers cast their first morsel to Tlaltecuhtli.
Their overlapping complexes share earth, purification, childbirth, medicine, flaying, cotton, and sweat-bath functions.
Shared flayed-skin imagery and festival correspondences connect their agricultural-renewal complexes.
They overlap in sexual, earth, fertility, iconographic, and calendrical functions.
Separate traditions give them complementary or competing sexual-fertility roles without a meeting.
The Tepeyac mother of the gods is called Tonantzin, though not explicitly equated elsewhere.
Toci is identified with Teteo Innan; connection to Tonantzin follows through the mother-of-gods title.
Comparative interpretations sometimes treat them as youthful and aged aspects of one goddess.
Interruption of solar order enables their feared descent; direct combat is unattested.
Xipe's sacrificial cult nourished or reenacted solar warfare through captive combat.

relations.myth: Solar journey on the Sun Stone
relations.note: Xiuhcoatl-like serpents frame, carry, or conduct the sun through cyclical time.
Xochiquetzal belongs to the divine group assembled when the gods die.
Modern synthesis portrays Xolotl guiding the sun through the underworld each night.
Xolotl evades sacrifice through transformations but is caught, enabling solar order.
The new sun remains motionless until the gods die; Xolotl evades that death.
Xochiquetzal and Piltzintecuhtli are named as Xochipilli’s parents.
relations.source: Histoyre du Mechique, Tetzcocan creation account

relations.note: Xochiquetzal and Piltzintecuhtli beget Xochipilli.

9 Wind.note: The Mixtec creator is a regional Quetzalcoatl-like analogue, not universally identical with the Mexica wind god.

Acxomocuil.note: Acxomocuil and Yacatecuhtli are listed together among merchant gods.

Amimitl.note: Later writers sometimes treated the aquatic-hunting gods as equivalent.

Apanecatl.note: Apanecatl joins Zolton and Cuilton in killing Mixcoatl.

Apantecuhtli.myth: Ambush of the four hundred Cloud Serpents
Apantecuhtli.note: Fellow younger Mimixcoatl who hides in water before their coordinated attack.

Atlatonan.note: A woman embodying Atlatonan ceremonially accompanies Tezcatlipoca's impersonator as a wife.
Atlatonan’s water-associated ixiptla was sacrificed in the ritual sequence preceding Toci’s central Ochpaniztli rites.

Black Tezcatlipoca.myth: The primordial pair generates four creator sons
Black Tezcatlipoca.note: Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl generate him as their second son.
Black Tezcatlipoca.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

Centzon Huitznahua.note: Taube proposes overlap between the two drunken, stellar, sacrificial collectives.
Coatlicue is mother of the collective Centzon Huitznahua.
They collectively plot to kill their pregnant mother but are defeated before harming her.
The Centzon Huitznahua are Coyolxauhqui's brothers in the Florentine genealogy.
Coyolxauhqui incites and leads her armed brothers up Coatepec against Coatlicue.
The Centzon Huitznahua are Huitzilopochtli's brothers in the Coatepec genealogy.
He pursues the attacking brothers around Coatepec and defeats them.
He kills many of the Four Hundred Southerners; only a remnant escapes south.
After defeating them, he takes their arms, equipment, and insignia.
Xiuhcoatl forms part of Huitzilopochtli's equipment during their rout and near-extermination.

Centzon Mimixcoa.myth: Ambush of the four hundred Cloud Serpents
Centzon Mimixcoa.note: Mixcoatl and four younger Mimixcoa ambush and destroy the disobedient stellar collective.
Iztac Mixcoatl recalls or revives the Cloud Serpents destroyed by Itzpapalotl.

Chalmēcacihuātl.note: The female merchant deity was honored and embodied alongside Yacatecuhtli.

Chicome Xochitl.note: Male artisans honor him while women artisans honor Xochiquetzal during the same feast.

Chicomexochitl.note: Ethnographers compare this living Huasteca maize power with Chicomecoatl without treating them as simply identical.

Chicōnquiāhuitl.note: Both gods were embodied by merchant-sponsored victims honored before sacrifice.

Chililico.note: Chililico and Macuilxochitl have ritual co-presence without a narrated interaction.
Chililico.source: Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites

Chimalman.note: Scholarship proposes a Chimalman–Coatlicue homolog based on miraculous motherhood and reconstructed ritual pairing.
They are commonly reconstructed as the paired deer-women who confront Xiuhnel and Mimich.
Mixcoatl pursues and shoots at Chimalman; their arrow-coded union produces Quetzalcoatl.

Cipactli.note: Some sources and retellings equate these overlapping earth-monster identities, while other colonial accounts distinguish them.

Cipactonal.myth: Creation of the first human couple
Cipactonal.note: Huitzilopochtli and Quetzalcoatl jointly create Cipactonal and give instructions concerning human life.
Cipactonal and Oxomoco divine that Nanahuatl can strike open Tonacatepetl.
A corrupt Telleriano commentary seemingly associates Patecatl with the primordial calendrical figure Cipactonal.

Citlalatonac.note: Citlalatonac is invoked after Chalchiuhtlicue’s washing when the infant is raised toward celestial powers.

Citlalicue.note: Citlalicue is invoked after Chalchiuhtlicue’s washing when the infant is raised toward celestial powers.
She is sometimes equated with Tonacacihuatl or Omecihuatl.
Citlalicue.source: Leyenda de los Soles and related cosmologies

Citlalinicue.note: Borbonicus figures identified as Citlalinicue are interpreted as her Tzitzimitl form.

Citlallatonac.note: Some scholarly mappings treat him as the male primordial parent.
Citlallatonac.source: Leyenda de los Soles and related cosmologies

Cochīmetl.note: Cochīmetl and Yacatecuhtli are listed together among merchant gods.

Cohuaxolotl.note: Captives impersonating Chantico and Cohuaxolotl are jointly sacrificed before the 1473 war.

Copil.note: Copil is Huitzilopochtli's nephew, the son of his sister Malinalxochitl.
Copil organizes enemies against the Mexica, and Huitzilopochtli directs the response.
Mexica agents kill Copil on Huitzilopochtli's command and remove or cast away his heart.

Coyōtl Īnāhual.note: Victims jointly embodied Coyōtl Īnāhual and Yacatecuhtli before sacrifice.

Cozcamiauh.note: Cozcamiauh is another name of Ilamatecuhtli-Tonan in the Tititl account.

Cuahuitlicac.note: He rejects the plot and indirectly protects Coatlicue by reporting the attackers' progress.
Cuahuitlicac defects from Coyolxauhqui's conspiracy and reports her army's advance to Huitzilopochtli.
Cuahuitlicac is one of the Huitznahua brothers in the Coatepec account.
Cuahuitlicac secretly reports each stage of the conspirators' advance to the unborn god.

Cuatlapanqui.note: He helps perfect pulque after Mayahuel discovers how to extract aguamiel.
Cuatlapanqui joins the specialists perfecting pulque after Patecatl finds its root.

Cuauhtlicoauh.myth: Ambush of the four hundred Cloud Serpents
Cuauhtlicoauh.note: Fellow younger Mimixcoatl who hides in a tree before their coordinated attack.

Cuetlachcihuatl.myth: Ambush of the four hundred Cloud Serpents
Cuetlachcihuatl.note: Female companion among the five who hides at the ballcourt before attacking.
She is presented as a possible sister among the five younger Mimixcoa.

Cuilton.note: Cuilton joins Apanecatl and Zolton in killing Mixcoatl.

Cuāuhtlaxayauh.note: Victims jointly embodied Cuāuhtlaxayauh and Yacatecuhtli before sacrifice.

Eagle.note: Eagle enters or approaches the fire after Nanahuatzin and the lunar candidate and becomes scorched.

Earth Mother.note: In a cognate trecena version, Earth Mother presents a captive to Tepeyollotl.

Guadalupe.note: Colonial and modern interpretations connect them through the shared maternal title Tonantzin.

Huehuecoyotl.note: He appears with the female transgressor sometimes identified as Xochiquetzal or Ixnextli.

Huemac.note: Tezcatlipoca's transformations provoke desire, commerce, dancing, war, and humiliation involving Huemac.

Huemac.myth: Huemac's ballgame with the rain gods
Huemac.note: The Tlaloque play ball against Huemac and lose, then offer him young maize.

Huemac.myth: Huemac rejects the rain gods' maize
Huemac.note: The Tlaloque punish Huemac's rejection of maize wealth with frost, drought, and crop failure.
A Tlaloque announces the Toltec order's decline and the coming establishment of Mexica rule.

Huixtocihuatl.note: A woman embodying Huixtocihuatl ceremonially accompanies Tezcatlipoca's impersonator as a wife.
Sahagún calls Huixtocihuatl the elder sister of the Tlaloque.
Huixtocihuatl is identified as the elder sister of the rain gods or Tlaloc complex.

Ichpochtli Tonantzin.note: Recent archaeological scholarship proposes this designation for a Tepeyac-area female cult; its antiquity remains debated.

Ihuimecatl.note: Ihuimecatl cooperates with Tezcatlipoca in deceptions against Quetzalcoatl and Tollan.

Ihuitl.note: Ihuitl is one of three hearth persons appointed to guard the offering.

Ilamatecuhtli.myth: Divine sequence of the maize life cycle
Ilamatecuhtli.note: Modern synthesis links Chicomecoatl with Ilamatecuhtli as mature and aged phases of maize.
Regional manuscripts’ aged festival patron is sometimes equated with Cihuacoatl.
Ilamatecuhtli is explicitly also called Tonan during the Tititl festival.
Her regalia and functions place her within the reconstructed nocturnal ancestral Tzitzimitl complex.

Ilancueitl.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl form an ancestral pair in migration genealogies.

Itztli.note: They appear in a shared sacrificial and obsidian configuration with disputed narrative meaning.
Almanacs link Itztli's obsidian knife and nocturnal judgment with Tezcatlipoca.
Telleriano-Remensis substitutes Itztli in a sequence where Tudela presents Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli.

Itztlotli.note: Itztlotli is sent as a messenger to question or negotiate with Tonatiuh.

Ixcuinameh.note: Tlazolteotl-Ixcuina is presented as a fourfold collective of goddesses.

Ixnextli.note: Commentators identify the female transgressor Ixnextli with Xochiquetzal, though witnesses differ.

Ixtlilton.note: Both gods have impersonators in the procession; their iconography also shows affinities.
Ixtlilton appears beside the Xochipilli-Cinteotl figure in the ballcourt scene.

Jaguar.note: Jaguar follows Eagle into or near the fire after the candidates and becomes spotted or scorched.

K’uk’ulkan.note: The Yucatec Feathered Serpent is a semantic counterpart linked through Postclassic exchange.

La Llorona.note: Later folklore and Chicana writing fuse her with Cihuacoatl’s wailing apparition.

Macuilcozcacuauhtli.note: Macuilcozcacuauhtli and Macuilxochitl appear together among the male pleasure and excess gods.

Macuilcuetzpalin.note: Macuilcuetzpalin and Macuilxochitl appear together among the male pleasure and excess gods.

Macuilmalinalli.note: Macuilmalinalli and Macuilxochitl appear together among the male pleasure and excess gods.

Macuiltochtli.note: Macuiltochtli and Macuilxochitl appear together among the male pleasure and excess gods.

Malinalxochitl.note: Malinalxochitl is Huitzilopochtli's sister in migration traditions.
He orders the migrants to abandon the dangerous sorceress while she sleeps.

Mary.note: Colonial Nahuatl worshippers and preachers applied Tonantzin to Mary at Guadalupe, an equation Sahagún contested.

Mayahuel’s grandmother.note: She pursues the transformed pair and helps destroy Mayahuel's branch.

Metztli.note: Metztli performs penance after Nanahuatl and falls into the ashes rather than the fire.

Mictecacihuatl.note: Later tellings place her beside Mictlantecuhtli, though the core Leyenda gives her little or no active role.
She is Mictlantecuhtli's wife and co-ruler in Mictlan.

Mictecacihuatl.myth: Retrieval of ancestral bones from Mictlan
Mictecacihuatl.note: Some modern retellings include her with Xolotl, without secure early attestation.

Mimich.note: A deer-woman pursues Mimich, who escapes by leaping into fire.

Mimixcoa.note: He orders the migrants to sacrifice the divine or ancestral Mimixcoa before assuming Mexica identity.
Mimixcoa.source: Historia de los mexicanos; Codex Aubin

Mixtec 9 Wind.note: Scholars equate this culture-founder with Quetzalcoatl through wind and Feathered Serpent traits.

Mixtecatl.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl are named as Mixtecatl's progenitors.

Nahui Tecpatl.myth: Variant creation of the second luminary
Nahui Tecpatl.note: This named second luminary occupies Tecciztecatl’s role in a related textual variant.

Nochpalliicue.myth: Sacrifice of the gods at Teotihuacan
Nochpalliicue.note: Nochpalliicue participates in the assembly and collective death demanded by the Sun.
Nochpalliicue is named among the goddesses assembled during the gods' mortality.

Otomitl.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl are named as Otomitl's progenitors.

Otontecuhtli.note: They share the same veintena ritual complex without a narrated meeting.

Oxomoco.myth: Creation of the first human couple
Oxomoco.note: Huitzilopochtli and Quetzalcoatl jointly create Oxomoco and give instructions concerning human life.
Oxomoco and Cipactonal divine that Nanahuatl can strike open Tonacatepetl.

Papaiztac.note: Papaiztac joins the specialists perfecting pulque after Patecatl finds its root.

Papaztac.note: He helps perfect pulque after Mayahuel discovers how to extract aguamiel.

Paynal.note: His lieutenant and mobile representative extends Huitzilopochtli's presence through a rapid ritual circuit.

Piltzintecuhtli.source: Histoyre du Mechique; Historia de los mexicanos

Piltzintecuhtli.note: An alleged adoptive-family connection arises only through the disputed parentage of Nanahuatzin.
Piltzintecuhtli is Nanahuatl's foster-father in the variant genealogy.
Later syntheses pair Tlazolteotl with Piltzintecuhtli as Cinteotl's parents.
Piltzintecuhtli and Xochiquetzal are named as Xochipilli’s parents.
Piltzintecuhtli.source: Histoyre du Mechique, Tetzcocan creation account

Piltzintecuhtli.note: He searches or mourns for Xochiquetzal while she sings from Tamoanchan.
Xochiquetzal is called his first wife, despite an internally conflicting creation account.
Piltzintecuhtli.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

Piltzintecuhtli.note: They couple in a cave and conceive Cinteotl.
They are partners who beget Xochipilli and foster Nanahuatzin.

Quetzalcoatl/Ehecatl.note: Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl leads the Tlaloque and sweeps their road because wind precedes rain.
Quetzalcoatl/Ehecatl.source: Florentine Codex and Nahuatl lexical citations

Quetzalpetlatl.note: The Tollan narrative calls Quetzalpetlatl Topiltzin's elder sister.
Topiltzin summons her; they drink pulque and violate their ascetic obligations.

Quilaztli.note: The text explicitly identifies Quilaztli as Cihuacoatl.
Cihuacoatl-Quilaztli is invoked as our mother and exacts death’s tribute in childbirth.

Q’uq’umatz.note: The K’iche’ creator belongs to a related Mesoamerican Feathered Serpent complex.

Red Tezcatlipoca.myth: The primordial pair generates four creator sons
Red Tezcatlipoca.note: Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl generate him as their first son.
Red Tezcatlipoca.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

Santa Muerte.note: Some modern devotees and writers equate them, but no continuous historical cultic identity is established.

Santiago.note: A Puebla oral tradition transfers Huitzilopochtli's armed miraculous birth to Santiago.

Teicu.note: The younger or second sister is one member of the Tlazolteotl-Ixcuina complex.

Tenoch.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl are named as Tenoch's progenitors.

Teoyaomiqui.note: León y Gama identified the colossal statue as Teoyaomiqui rather than Coatlicue.
Teoyaomiqui.source: Descripción histórica y cronológica de las dos piedras

Tepictoton.note: The small ritual mountain bodies are treated as Tlaloque or embodiments of their divine mountains.

Tepoztecatl.note: He helps perfect pulque after Mayahuel discovers how to extract aguamiel.

Tepuztecatl.note: After Patecatl finds the root, Tepuztecatl helps perfect pulque-making.

Tezcacoatl.note: Tezcacoatl carries Huitzilopochtli's sacred bundle as the god's designated bearer.

The Four Hundred Mimixcoa.note: Itzpapalotl attacks and devours the collective ancestral hunters.

The assembled gods at Teotihuacan.note: Ehecatl sacrifices the assembled gods because their deaths are required for solar motion.

Tiacapan.note: The firstborn sister is one member of the fourfold Tlazolteotl-Ixcuina complex.

Tlacahuepan.note: Tlacahuepan and Macuilxochitl have ritual co-presence without a narrated interaction.
Tlacahuepan.source: Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites

Tlacahuepan Cuexcotzin.note: A separate large tzoalli image accompanies Huitzilopochtli; its precise identity remains disputed.

Tlaco.note: The middle sister is one member of the fourfold Tlazolteotl-Ixcuina complex.

Tlalcihuatl.note: A colonial cosmogonic tradition pairs them as male and female earth powers, though their separateness varies.

Tlalli Iyollo.note: Tlalli Iyollo is explicitly another name of Teteo Innan and Toci.

Tlantepozilamatl.note: Tlantepozilamatl raises or guards Nanahuatl and associated children before conflict over her diversion of food.

Tlilhua.note: Tlilhua joins the specialists perfecting pulque after Patecatl finds its root.

Tlilhuah.note: He helps perfect pulque after Mayahuel discovers how to extract aguamiel.

Tlotepe.myth: Ambush of the four hundred Cloud Serpents
Tlotepe.note: Fellow younger Mimixcoatl who hides within a mountain before their attack.

Tochancalqui.note: At Huitzilopochtli's command, Tochancalqui ignites Xiuhcoatl for the coming attack.

Toltecatl.note: Toltecatl cooperates with Tezcatlipoca in deceptions against Quetzalcoatl and Tollan.

Tonacatepetl.note: The Tlaloque break or blast open the food mountain and release its agricultural stores.

Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl.note: A woman named Xochiquetzal is introduced into his chamber and causes his fall.

Tozpan.note: Tozpan is one of three hearth persons appointed to guard the offering.

Tzapotlatenan.note: Sahagún says Toci at the Tlaxcala-area sanctuary was called Tzapotlatenan, a medical and steam-bath deity.

Tzocaca.note: He helps perfect pulque after Mayahuel discovers how to extract aguamiel.
Tzocaca joins the specialists perfecting pulque after Patecatl finds its root.

Tzontemoc.note: Colonial sources sometimes conjoin this ninth-underworld lord with Mictlantecuhtli, but the identity remains disputed.

Ulmecatl.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl are named as Ulmecatl's progenitors.

Xelhua.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl are named as Xelhua's progenitors.

Xicalancatl.note: Iztac Mixcoatl and Ilancueitl are named as Xicalancatl's progenitors.

Xilonen.note: Xilonen's impersonator is killed at Cinteotl's temple.
Some sources treat Xilonen as Chicomecoatl’s name or youthful maize phase; others distinguish them.
Their divine impersonators co-occur within disputed accounts of festival sacrifice.
A woman embodying Xilonen ceremonially accompanies Tezcatlipoca's impersonator as a wife.

Xiuhnel.note: A deer-woman identified contextually as Itzpapalotl entices Xiuhnel into a sexual encounter.
The deer-woman devours Xiuhnel after their sexual encounter.

Xocotl.note: Yacatecuhtli and four other divine embodiments were honored with Xocotl.

Xocotzin.note: The youngest sister is one member of the fourfold Tlazolteotl-Ixcuina complex.

Xomoco.note: A colonial gloss says Xomoco was her name before she became Itzpapalotl.

Yacapitzāhuac.note: One Sahaguntine passage calls the merchant deity Yacapitzahuac or Yiacatecuhtli.

Yapalicue.note: Yapalicue is named among the goddesses assembled during the gods' mortality.

Yapaliicue.myth: Sacrifice of the gods at Teotihuacan
Yapaliicue.note: Yapaliicue participates in the assembly and collective death demanded by the Sun.

Yoalticitl.note: The steam-bath effigy or medical manifestation is identified with Toci, though its independent identity remains uncertain.

Yohualtecuhtli.note: Modern scholarship proposes Yohualtecuhtli as Tonatiuh's nocturnal or underworld aspect.

Zolton.note: Zolton joins Apanecatl and Cuilton in killing Mixcoatl.

dead male warriors.note: Warriors escort the morning sun; the Cihuateteo perform the western portion.

the Mimixcoa.note: They share the same veintena ritual complex without a narrated meeting.

the assembled gods.myth: Divine autosacrifice creates humanity from ancestral bones
the assembled gods.note: The gods bleed over bones formerly held by Mictlantecuhtli, without confronting him directly.

the four Tezcatlipocas.note: Some colonial summaries make the four primordial creator gods Tlaloc’s creators.

the gods.note: The gods join Quetzalcoatl in penitential bloodletting over the ground bones.

the gods.myth: Gods sacrifice themselves for solar motion
the gods.note: The gods choose death to revive the stationary Sun and sustain humanity.

the gods collectively.note: Horrified gods compensate Tlaltecuhtli by making useful plants and terrestrial features arise from the body.
